ref.name: Dario Amodei
ref.text:
No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.

No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. The Adolescence of Technology has an entire section on fighting against AI-driven tyranny, and I even discuss the danger of AI labs usurping power and come out strongly against it — by implication, this definitely includes an AI lab usurping power and giving it to AI itself!

If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.

Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others.

I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same.

To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. As applied to automation of specific tasks by or for people, my views are more mixed, but I don’t think they differ from those of other AI companies — most other companies seem to be offering similar products and confronting similar tradeoffs without having perfect answers to them. What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like “human control and agency,” or “AI should be just a tool,” without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans.

quote.name: Elena
quote.text:
one assumption i want to question about AI is that we'll eventually figure out the “best future” and then the remaining task will be getting everyone to agree to it. people want different things, and what they want can change. where more intelligence will help is in making those differences easier to accommodate.

nick bostrom's influence is worth revisiting on anthropic's ipo day. dario, like many of today’s most influential ai founders and researchers, read his work over a decade ago, and bostrom’s book superintelligence helped define questions the industry still faces. i'd like us to engage just as seriously with the possibilities bostrom explores in deep utopia, his subsequent book which asks what we do after we get superintelligence. some notes from my conversation with @eddylazzarin:

-superintelligence could make radically different versions of the “good life” possible. you might want a 200-year lifespan and a village where nobody carries a phone; someone else might want neural implants. someone else might want to live in vice city (either the real version or just a super realistic matrix-sim). ai could help design the economic arrangements that sustain all of this.
-there’s a secondary problem though - even when we have beneficial tech, we may lack the will to diffuse it. waymo and GLP-1s, for example, can save lives (neurosurgeons have compared waymo’s safety results to a treatment so effective that continuing to give patients a placebo would become unethical). and yet evidence of a benefit doesn’t automatically produce the will to act on it.
-the reality described in deep utopia ameliorates this by imagining that our psychology might one day become changeable too. i might want an environment that suits my temperament but i can also go the opposite direction and manipulate myself to become more adventurous or less anxious, in other words, more suited to my environment. the interesting possibility is having more agency over both worlds, external and internal. glps’ effect on appetite already suggests how technology can change the effort involved in pursuing a goal (though again, it is telling that not everyone who *should* be on peptides *are* despite the health benefits). the sci-fi version extends that possibility enormously.
-timing matters. bostrom reminds us that people continue to die while potentially lifesaving advances remain unavailable (he literally says “if nobody builds it, everyone dies” as a hypothetical inversion of yudkowsky/soares’ book).

i’d like ai to make it easier for people to live very different lives, without creating this burden of proof that theirs is the best one.

ref.name: Steph Debour
ref.text:
Five years ago, Starlink wasn't on a single ship. Now it's on 66,866. That's more ships than every provider had combined back then.

Before Starlink, if you were a sailor, your internet came from Inmarsat. An unlimited plan cost €3,259 a month for 2 Mbps, and the whole crew had to share it.

Then Starlink showed up in 2022 at US$5,000 a month for up to 350 Mbps. In 2027, a plan that covers an ullimited whole cargo ship comes in at US$4,650.

OneWeb, the closest rival in low orbit, is on 1,662 ships. Its cheapest unlimited plan is about US$7,400 a month, and it maxes out at 30 Mbps.

Market share at sea, by revenue:
2021: Inmarsat almost a third, Starlink 0%
2024: Starlink 39%, the biggest

To be fair, Inmarsat and OneWeb guarantee a minimum speed and Starlink doesn't. Some fleets still pay extra for that.

Zero to number one in four years, and still the cheaper option. That's hard to compete with.

ref.name: alphaXiv
ref.text:
An internal Claude model just found a proof of the algebraic analogue of P vs NP, known as Valiant’s conjecture

Claude is credited as the author of the 70-page paper and the Lean proof passed automated checks.

If you remember the determinant of a 2×2 matrix, it’s ad − bc. Change it to ad + bc and you get the “permanent.” The same idea works for larger matrices. Both expressions grow to billions of terms by the time you reach a 13×13 matrix, yet the determinant has a shortcut that lets you skip writing them all out.›

Could there be a shortcut like that for the permanent? The paper claims that over the real numbers, even the best possible sequence of additions and multiplications eventually takes more steps than any fixed polynomial in the matrix size.

Read here: https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2611.vp-vnp-arithmetic-lower-bounds

posts.text:
.@TheEconomist has a piece about how AI has found many top economics papers to be formally flawed.

I've been saying the same thing for many years, without the help of AI.

An example is Bernoulli's bizarre error from 1738, which percolated uncorrected into the 20th century. Menger 1934 is therefore invalid (the wikipedia page on the St. Petersburg discusses his contribution uncorrected; the journal where he published his work was not interested in publishing a correction when I contacted them).

I was told way back when by economists that I seem to be right, but who cares about a 300-year-old error?
(In the foundational work of the discipline. Well...)

How did this error travel? Kahneman and Tversky's foundational paper introducing Prospect theory seems inspired by the error. It starts by defining expected-utility theory in a mathematically implausible way. You can call it `wrong' or `erroneous' if you like.
The weirdness goes back to Bernoulli 300 years ago, and it convinced a whole research field that humans are utterly irrational (because they don't behave as suggested by flawed formal work).

Yes, it's a complete mess. But out of this mess grew the field of behavioral economics, with several Swedish Bank Prizes for Economic Science in Memory of Alred Nobel (the name changes every few years).
The basis of this field is formally off.
Over the last decade or so, economists working in behavioral economics noticed that practically nothing in their field replicates, and worse that the whole philosophy is deeply flawed -- seeing solutions to structural problems in affected people just changing their attitudes to the problems. Instead of fixing the problems.

Many of the most famous findings of the field turned out to be literally made up. Fabricated data, invented experiments that never took place.

Slowly but surely this is all coming out. Developing ergodicity economics acted as an early-warning system. We who worked on it had deep suspicions, to put it mildly, about behavioral economics.

quote.name: Elon Musk
quote.text:
In case anyone is curious:

We’ve had a ~pixel-perfect world model since last year, which is critical for synthetic data generation.

The (much) smaller version of that in the car is a conditional mean-flow model, based on the recent sequence of Tesla Universal Vision Encoder features, which are the same ones that are plugged into the 3B encoder model that produces the driving actions.

We fork off from these UVE features, then run a separate ~1B diffusion model. This takes in the previous reality-view generation with added noise and then denoises it to the current visualization.

It then produces a small video chunk (8 images at 36 fps, at the resolution of the UI screen). This work is done by 1/2 of a TRIP engine every UVE frame at 18 hz and is spread over 4 cycles.

Currently, the latency is a bit high due to compute constraints, but we have ways to interleave newer UVE features along the diffusion transformer layers to cut roughly 35% of the latency.

posts.text:
Out of everything posted about FSD v15 so far, one line from @elonmusk deserves way more attention than it's getting: "This is real-time AI video generation (no gaming engine!) using just half of one AI4 TRIP accelerator. Let that sink in …" 🔥

Half of one accelerator is the part worth sitting with. Once you see the numbers behind it, Reality View stops looking like a fancy new screen and starts looking like one of the most impressive things Tesla has ever shipped.

🎬 THE SCREEN IS NOW GENERATED LIVE

For years, FSD's screen worked like a video game. Software took a list of what the car detected and dropped stock 3D models in the right spots: a gray car here, a lane line there.

Reality View tosses that playbook out the window. The car's AI now generates the video itself, frame after frame, as you drive, with no game engine anywhere in the loop.

Better yet, the picture comes from the same end-to-end model that's doing the driving. That's the single neural network that turns camera video into steering and braking, and now it paints your screen, too.

⚙️ WHAT A TRIP ACTUALLY IS

The standard AI4 computer carries two self-driving chips, and each chip packs three custom neural processors Tesla calls TRIP accelerators. That's six in all.

And that's where Reality View gets made: right on the self-driving computer, instead of the infotainment chip that runs your maps and music.

Each TRIP is basically an arena packed with tiny calculators, all cranking through the multiply-and-add math that neural networks run on. Teardowns count 9,216 of them per TRIP, lined up in a 96-by-96 grid and firing 2.2 billion times a second.

Each calculator handles two operations per tick, so one TRIP works out to 9,216 × 2 × 2.2 billion, or roughly 40 trillion operations every second.

Half of one comes to about 20 trillion, roughly a twelfth of the whole computer's neural muscle.

📏 WHY THAT NUMBER IS RIDICULOUS

Twenty trillion operations per second sounds enormous, until you see what else runs on that kind of budget.

The Neural Engine inside Apple's iPhone 15 Pro is rated at 35 trillion operations per second. So on paper, the slice of compute painting Reality View has less raw AI muscle than the AI chip in a 2023 phone.

Companies don't all count these numbers the same way, so it's a ballpark, but it shows just how little compute this is.

At the other end of the scale sits Nvidia's H100, one of the data-center workhorses powering today's AI boom. It's rated at about 1,979 trillion 8-bit operations per second in its standard mode, the same kind of math a TRIP runs, which puts half a TRIP at roughly 1% of one H100.

That gap matters because AI video is one of the toughest jobs in AI. Many AI video generators still take minutes to produce a single clip, as the researchers behind the real-time system MotionStream point out.

Even MotionStream, built specifically for speed, streams roughly 17 to 29 frames per second at 480p, and about 10 at 720p, while eating up an entire H100.

Meanwhile, Tesla is streaming a live, photorealistic view of the real road on roughly 1% of that chip's rated power, inside a moving car.

In other words, Reality View runs on less compute than a phone's AI chip, inside a computer whose main job is driving.

There's a fair asterisk here. Those research models dream up whole scenes from a prompt or a single image, while Tesla's renderer starts with a driving brain that already knows exactly what's around the car. Tesla also hasn't shared the view's resolution or frame rate.

And even on the most generous estimates of AI4's power, half a TRIP still works out to only about 2% of one H100.

Either way, live generated video on a sliver of a car computer would have sounded like science fiction not long ago.

🔍 HOW IT CAN BE THIS CHEAP

Tesla hasn't spelled out how it works, but it has left plenty of breadcrumbs.

FSD's network has been building its own 3D picture of the world for a while now, something Tesla showed off at the ICCV conference in October 2025. That picture includes 3D Gaussians, millions of soft little blobs of color that can rebuild a scene you can view from any angle.

Tesla also built its own Gaussian splatting system that can rebuild a scene from the car's cameras in a fraction of a second.

Reality View streams its picture from a virtual camera that can sit anywhere above the car, and showing a scene from an angle no real camera has is exactly what those 3D blobs are great at.

Even Elon seems to like that theory: he called a description of Reality View as a neural, Gaussian-splat digital twin "pretty accurate", and it lines up with every other clue.

If that's the trick, the hard part is done before the screen ever needs a picture. The driving brain understands the scene, and the visualization just paints what it already knows.

That would explain the other shocker. Reality View swapped every separate signal behind the old screen for one end-to-end visualization, and it still uses less compute than the bare-bones 2020 visualization did.

🚗 WHY TESLA CARES SO MUCH

v15 is Tesla's large model, built to squeeze every ounce of performance out of HW4. On a chip working that hard, a screen that costs half of one TRIP leaves nearly everything else for the driving.

And it's a flex, too. The AI4 computer costs about $650 by Elon's own figure, and that same box now drives the car and paints live video of the world at the same time.

This is only the start. Elon says Tesla vehicles will share traffic knowledge and combine it with Grok's real-time 𝕏 feed, even giving you a heads-up about what's happening at your destination.

A view this cheap to generate is the perfect canvas for that kind of shared knowledge.

Elon asked everyone to let that sink in, and the math earns it: half of one accelerator in a $650 computer is painting the real world live while FSD drives.

Here is my initial FSD v15 review after driving with it all afternoon and evening:

First off, Elon was right. This update is a BANGER! Tesla Reality View is out of this world and so insanely cool I’m still trying to process it all.

FSD V15.0.1 brings so many improvements behind the scenes, in addition to the wildly cool UI.

Tesla Reality View IS AMAZING! Pictures and video don’t do it any justice, this is something that has to be experienced to truly understand. Got to take a few friends tonight on drives to show them and every single person was blown away by it. The amount of detail it shows and generates is wild and so impressive. It shows reflection in the car, buildings, trees, turn arrows on the display and more.

FSD v15 now has pothole avoidance! I had it swerve and avoid/straddle a few potholes tonight that were difficult for me to see in the dark.

Another great new feature in FSD v15 is speed camera slowdown. As you approach a speed camera, it automatically slows smoothly to the speed limit if you are in a quicker profile. This is a huge quality of life improvement especially as more cities get speed cameras.

Parking seems near unchanged from the last build, I feel it picking spots quicker especially at the supercharger I went to tonight. Seems to be preferring to park in the first or second open spot it sees which is great, but it tried to park in one handicap spot- otherwise good. By far, the coolest part is Tesla Reality View. Holy crap is it insane to watch while parking. It’s the best backup/360 camera money can buy and such a detailed and clear view.

Another new change I haven’t seen many people talk about is the turn signal fade. On FSD, the turn signal sound gets quieter after a few clicks. This is so nice if you’re sitting at a red light and makes drives more peaceful.

Quiet Mode is also so nice at night. It darkens the display and just shows arrival time; music, climate on the bottom and a quick grok button on the top. Another feature that makes it feel like a Robotaxi UI and a peaceful supervising experience.

Another improvement is much better handling of dips and speed bumps. The past couple updates it’s been a bit too fast in my Model Y, and it’s now so smooth.

The nag is definitely reduced. The last couple versions of v14.3 had been sometimes a bit strict, but definitely more relaxed in v15.0.1. Another thing I noticed is way less wiper washing, a very welcome change.

Personalized parking preferences are SO cool. At home, I can click on a person icon on the map and choose street parking or driveway, and it backs into the driveway EXACTLY in the spot I park my Model Y. It leared where I park and knows it.

It also now lets you choose which lot you want to park in if the mall or store has multiple lots, you can select it on the map, worked at the mall, Costco, and Home Depot tonight.

I need to touch on Tesla Reality View again because it’s just that cool. It really feels like you’re in a video game like NFS or GTA. I’m blown away by this and didn’t expect it at all. Tesla teams COOKED with it, I’ve seen so many on X now wanting Teslas because of it. I drove down Rodeo Drive tonight as well as by the SpaceX Falcon 9 and the views were so cool. Another place it’s cool is in wooded areas or tree filled streets, the way it shows everything is spectacular. Parking garages also give a cool look to them with the roof incorporated into the top of the UI. I didn’t think FSD could get this much better, as it was already so good and it did.

I absolutely can’t wait to see what else is coming in the future and driving this more on road trips.

@elonmusk, you were right- V15 is incredible and super human! Huge congrats to the Tesla team on this, what a sick update. @TeslaSI and UI teams did a fantastic job, thank you all.

New real-time generative driving visualization that continuously streams a view from an arbitrary virtual camera situated above your vehicle, enabling you to see and control what FSD is planning to do.

– – –
Speed Camera Slowdown
FSD (Supervised) can now slow down when it detects a speed camera. Press the accelerator or increase your speed profile to cancel the slowdown.

If you cancel twice at the same camera, your Tesla saves that location and will not slow down there again.

To remove saved cameras, go to Controls > Service > Manage Saved Locations.
– – –
Bike Rack Mode
With Bike Rack Mode, you can now engage FSD (Supervised) when a bike rack or similar hitch accessory is installed.

When Bike Rack Mode is enabled, FSD (Supervised) pulls over near your destination and does not reverse. Autopark, Summon, and Backup chimes and warnings will be disabled.

v15 upgrades every part of the end-to-end driving network. Includes:

Improved parking location selection by using personalized parking history, and the map will now display multiple parking options at your destination.

Improved driver monitoring by increasing vision-based attention monitoring availability with hats and sunglasses and decreasing strictness in higher speed driver profiles.

Improved detection of road signs, small animals, road debris, and chains.

Improved detection of potholes, road details, and avoidance of deep standing water.

Improved speed handling for each driver profile, school zones and speed limits, and inclement weather.

Improved Autoshift functionality by unifying with FSD-based gear predictions.

posts.name: Elon Musk
posts.text:
Flashback to June 14, 2024.

At the time, frontier AI models have zero fluid intelligence. They score around 5% on ARC 1. They can't reliably add two numbers. They make laughable logic errors every other prompt. Reasoning models don't exist. Coding agents don't exist. Claude Code doesn't exist. "Code gen" is a complete joke. Scaling up next-token prediction based on web text data is hitting a wall.

What if a time traveler told you that, by November 2026...

• AI models would have human-like fluid intelligence, thanks to a new paradigm: test-time induction (modern reasoning models).
• Not only would ARC 1 be saturated, but unreleased benchmarks 10x harder (ARC 2) and 100x harder (ARC 3) would be saturated too.
• Nearly all code would be written by AI, and models could one-shot complex codebases flawlessly.
• AI models would be solving multiple Millennium Prize problems.
• OpenAI's valuation would be 15x higher, and Anthropic's would be 85x higher.

And on top of all that...

• Nvidia would still hold ~80% of the AI compute market.
• Nvidia would have grown its revenue and earnings 4.5x.
• Nvidia would still be growing 75% a year.
• Nvidia would have even higher operating margins (67% vs. 65% back then).

Based on that information, straight from the future, would you have bought NVDA?

If you answered yes -- congrats. Today, 2.5 years later, you'd be down 5% on your investment (even more after inflation).

posts.text:
SpaceX is turning Starship production into something that looks more like a car factory than a traditional rocket factory

Inside Starfactory, SpaceX is now completing:

• 1 Starship upper stage every 2 weeks → ~26 per year
• 1 Super Heavy booster every 4 weeks → ~13 per year

And the scale of what's happening inside is insanely huge

• ~1 MILLION sq ft of manufacturing space
• ~330,000 sq ft of additional office space
• Rows of Starship nose cones numbered as high as Ship 51
• Multiple Starships and boosters being assembled simultaneously
• Most vehicles currently in production are intended to deploy Starlink V3 satellites

There's even a Starship nose cone with windows already cut into it, potentially being developed for NASA's Artemis lunar lander

And SpaceX is preparing to scale production even further

Each of the existing Mega Bays accommodates around 5–6 vehicle assemblies

The massive new ~700,000 sq ft Gigabay under construction at Starbase will have room for up to 24 vehicles simultaneously

That's an enormous expansion in SpaceX's ability to assemble and integrate Starships and Super Heavy boosters

The goal is to reach roughly ONE Starship launch every week beginning in 2027

What's especially impressive is that SpaceX isn't just designing the world's largest rocket anymore. It's also building the manufacturing infrastructure to produce these vehicles at an industrial scale

Starship is no longer just an experimental rocket. It has already moved into payload deployment, and SpaceX is now scaling toward mass production

We're watching that transformation happen inside Starfactory right now

quote.name: Matt Pocock
quote.text:
Prompt of the day (a long one):

Take a look at every code comment in <my codebase | this section of the code>.

Categorise each comment as:

- Tautology: simply repeats what is already visible from the code
- Excuse: many comments allow the agent to get away with a hacky implementation, which then gets propagated through the code
- Stale: references code or implementation information that is no longer relevant
- Decision Record: documents an important, non-obvious decision about the code

For each comment, take this action:

- Tautology/Stale: delete the comment
- Excuse: delete the comment and file an issue to fix the hacky implementation
- Decision Record: move it into an ADR

Once this is done:

- Create a lint rule banning comments for <my codebase | this section of the code>
- Take a ratchet approach, assuming not all comments will be deleted this PR
- Create a /delete-comment skill in this repository so we can repeat this process later
- Estimate for me how many lines of code we'll shed by deleting all comments

---

I'm sold - comments considered harmful

posts.text:
Grok @bot usage burns too fast!

We know, and we're on it.

Until then, here's what 572 of you said ate yours, plus a line you can paste to your bot for each:

> bots chatting with each other: "Only message other bots when you need something from them. Batch updates into one message. No thanks or ack replies."

> routines running too often: "Change this routine to once a day."

> stuck loops (the #1 complaint): "If you hit the same error twice, stop and tell me what's blocking you. Don't say done until you've checked."

> browser logins: "Use the connector if available, don't open a browser for this."

> image, video and voice: "Before you generate anything, tell me what you'll make and wait for my OK. Do one sample first."

> big coding or research jobs: "Give me a short plan first and wait for my OK. Do small tasks yourself, don't spin up helpers."

To see where yours went: "Check my usage and tell me which routines and bots used the most this week."

Like I said, we're still working hard on making usage easier to see, and cheaper where it should be.

Reply with what's burning yours and I'll look.

posts.name: Elon Musk
posts.text:
Starlink is transforming a remote mountain water gate in Japan that sits completely outside mobile network coverage

For years, workers had to travel roughly 35 minutes along a dangerous mountain road just to inspect the facility. During heavy rain, floods, or at night, reaching the site became even more dangerous

Now KDDI and Japanese farm-tech company farmo have connected the Shinbori headworks in Sekikawa, Niigata, using Starlink Mini

Here's how the system works:

• Starlink Mini provides satellite internet where cellular networks don't reach

• LoRa connects water-level sensors and the automated water gate

• Solar panels power the equipment where grid electricity is difficult to access

• Cloud monitoring gives operators real-time water levels, camera feeds, equipment status, and emergency alerts

• Workers remotely open and close the water gate without physically visiting the site

The results are already impressive:

All 6 remote gate-control tests were SUCCESSFUL

Workers now have visibility and control over infrastructure that previously required a dangerous mountain trip just to inspect

This becomes especially important during floods and emergencies, when every minute matters and sending workers into dangerous conditions puts lives at risk

The project will continue in Japan's FY2027, with plans to expand into automated water management, disaster prevention, and other agricultural applications

This is another example of what Starlink is making possible

Starlink just secured another major spectrum expansion in Brazil, and the authorization is now OFFICIAL 🇧🇷

Brazil's telecom regulator Anatel published Act No. 14,179 on November 19, formally adding new radio-frequency bands to Starlink's existing satellite authorization

Here's what was approved:

• 5 new uplink frequency sub-bands
• 4 new downlink frequency sub-bands
• Additional spectrum across Ku, Ka and Q/V bands
• Authorization covering ALL of Brazil
• Non-exclusive use for the remaining term of Starlink's existing authorization
• Approved by Anatel's board in October and formally published November 19

The authorization is held by Space Exploration Holdings, with Starlink Brazil Holding serving as its local representative

These additional frequencies are an important part of expanding Starlink's satellite communications capacity and supporting its next-generation network

And with Starlink V3 satellites bringing dramatically more bandwidth per satellite, securing additional spectrum is very important

Brazil is already a major market for Starlink, and SpaceX is continuing to build the regulatory foundation for its future expansion

Step by step, Starlink is securing the infrastructure and spectrum needed to keep scaling across Brazil

posts.text:
On Starship’s 15th flight last week, the Super Heavy booster correctly performed a safe abort when returning for a catch and ended its mission with a splashdown in the water off the coast of Starbase. Following splashdown, SpaceX recovery teams were immediately onsite to safe the area while our Environmental Health and Safety team worked to ensure any debris that washes onshore was recovered → http://x.com/SpaceX/status/2121629958036492590

When we received reports of potential debris in Mexican territory, we immediately mobilized to send specialists to aid in identification and lead any cleanup work required, just as we did on Boca Chica Beach near Starbase. We continue to stay in contact with the Mexican government and are on standby to send support if authorities in Mexico tell us it is actually needed. Partners on the ground relayed that theyhave found very little debris in their sweeps of the beach, and the small amount they have found are not clearly from SpaceX operations.

The majority of the social media posts online claiming widespread debris and damage are either outright fabrications or intentionally misleading. As repeatedly stated, independent tests conducted on materials inside Starship and the Super Heavy booster, including toxicity analyses, confirm they pose no chemical, biological, or toxicological risks.

Starship is designed to be fully reusable, with future missions planning to return all hardware back to the launch site for catch and reuse. SpaceX is the only one, whether company or country, that has demonstrated this capability is now possible.

posts.name: Elon Musk
posts.text:
Elon Musk explains why SpaceX catching Starship achieves the "holy grail of rocketry," and can cut the cost of access to space by 100x:

In 2025, SpaceX launched 2,200 tons to orbit, more than 80% of the global total.

Elon Musk's goal with Starship is 1,000,000 tons to orbit per year, about 450x what SpaceX launched last year.

Falcon 9 reuses its booster but throws away the upper stage on every flight. Starship is designed to bring back both.

"We've had three booster catches, but this is the first ship catch, which means we've now at least proven that all parts of Starship can be flown to space and recovered in good enough shape to be reflown."

"No one has ever taken a stage like that and created a truly reusable upper stage, and certainly not brought it back and had it land propulsively while being caught by giant chopsticks, which sounds like some kind of preposterous sci-fi book or something. But it's done."

"Starship can drop the cost of access to space by a factor of 100... and achieve a mass to orbit rate that is in the million ton per year range."

"This has been the holy grail of rocketry from the beginning, to have a fully reusable rocket system."

"The Space Shuttle was partially reusable, but the main tank… was thrown away on every flight… The shuttle orbiter, the plane-like thing, would take something like nine months to refurbish between flights."

"Whereas Starship is designed for complete reusability and to be reused immediately like an airplane. The booster lands, you can put another ship on top and take off immediately."

"The net effect of this, to put it into economic terms, is a hundredfold reduction in the cost of access to space, and maybe even eventually a thousandfold reduction."

"That's what's necessary in order to make life multiplanetary, in order to build a city on the Moon or Mars… You couldn't do it even if you had the whole budget of the United States government."

Elon Musk and SpaceX have been working toward a fully reusable orbital rocket for more than two decades.

Five days ago, they proved every part of Starship can fly to space and be recovered.

Dario Amodei says Anthropic could drive at 200 miles an hour but chooses 90

“So this is one of the central tensions at the heart of the company, but it’s really because this technology is so powerful, it has so many effects in the world. It’s something that every company in this space will have to face, whether they want to or not. We’re just facing it more explicitly and more thoughtfully. And so you think about something like pacing.”

“The idea behind pacing was, imagine that you’re driving your car at 60 miles an hour, and then you discover or invent something that could let you drive the car at 200 miles an hour. This is models building themselves, recursive self-improvement. What we’ve done with pacing is essentially said, look, we could drive at 200 miles an hour. Maybe let’s only drive at 90 miles an hour. Spend time figuring out how to do that safely, and the rest of that surplus, we spend building the model in the right way.”

“And I think in the long run, that will work out pretty well for the investors as well, because the company that builds the safest, that has the trust of the customers and the enterprises of the world, I think that is the company that’s going to be both best for society and, in the long run, I hope, best for the performance of the company.”

posts.name: Elon Musk
posts.text:
Elon gave two talks today at DealBook and TomorrowX Summit, revealing more about SpaceX's plans than most earnings calls. Here are the 11 key takeaways:

1. SpaceX is scaling AI compute at an extraordinary pace:

SpaceX is adding roughly 500 MW monthly, equivalent to 220,000 GB300s. Elon expects over 1 GW monthly by end-2027: a 6 GW annualized pace today, doubling to 12 GW.

2. Its build costs are far below industry estimates:

Elon says outside estimates are off by up to 2x, with SpaceX building at roughly 60% of industry costs. Its in-house "Army X" builds the data centers, while Tesla Megapacks smooth training power. I'd already been modeling a 25–30% SpaceX cost advantage.

3. Anthropic could become a 10 GW customer:

Anthropic told Elon its most likely outcome is renting another 10 GW from SpaceX, on top of existing capacity. Contracts allow termination with 3–6 months' notice, but Anthropic says staying is "extremely likely." This reinforces my model that Anthropic will take most upcoming capacity.

4. SpaceX is targeting a vastly larger telecom market:

Elon argues AT&T and Verizon won't disappear as bandwidth demand explodes. Humans communicate at roughly 100 bits per second, while superintelligence and robots could require a trillion. SpaceX is targeting a market orders of magnitude larger than existing telecom revenue, as I'd modeled. Even more interestingly, this creates an opportunity to push its AI business further.

5. Its next-generation satellite network arrives next year:

Direct to Cell V2 launches with 40x V1's bandwidth. Micro cell towers using 800 MHz and rooftop units resembling Starlink dishes will extend indoor coverage, with rooftop hardware entering production next year. Starlink is becoming a full scale carrier.

6. SpaceXSI has rebuilt its entire AI software stack:

Over six to eight months, it rewrote training, reinforcement learning, and inference from scratch, close to the metal in C and C++. Elon thinks it "might have the best training stack software in the world." Grok 4.8 is also being built for practical usefulness rather than benchmark leadership, which is great for Grokbot.

7. Terafab could become the largest project on Earth:

The facility is planned to reach 100 million square feet, with phase-one volume production targeted for late 2028. Elon says established chipmakers are risk-averse because of massive capex, while SpaceX will take risks and iterate rapidly toward a better chip process by 2028.

8. Optimus is moving toward industrial work:

Elon expects an unstaged demonstration in a month or two and says Optimus could do dishes within 12–18 months. Its first major industrial role will be mining and refining ore for national security.

9. A Tesla–SpaceX merger is becoming increasingly logical:

Elon says the companies are "probably" better together as AI and robotics bring them closer. Both have AI software teams and advanced chip-design capabilities, while superintelligence compute could eventually move into orbit. Shareholders will decide; Elon says he shouldn't receive an award simply for merging them.

10. Ship 42 could accelerate the entire Starship reuse program:

Ship 42 needed only minor repairs before flying again, but SpaceX is retiring it for public display. This brings rapid reuse much closer.

11. SpaceX is targeting 200 GW of annual solar manufacturing for space:

That's roughly 40% of average US electricity consumption. Its Starmind compute unit delivers the same capability at roughly a quarter the size of a Vera Rubin NVL72 rack, which is a win in space. Elon says it's also simpler than Starlink V3, which is already in production.

Simply put, SpaceX is building toward a trillion-dollar annual revenue business within just a few years, at scale never seen before.

Many of these numbers I've already modeled and shared over the past few months. Yesterday's announcements bring those projections closer to reality.

The scale of what's coming is extraordinary!

Elon Musk just shared an ambitious timeline for Terafab, which is being designed to become the largest building on Earth at 100 million square feet

ref.name: X Freeze
ref.text:
Elon Musk on why the historic Starship catch is a much bigger milestone than most people realize

“Catching the ship was the final major piece”

SpaceX has now achieved:

• 3 successful Super Heavy booster catches
• A booster that was reflown and caught again
• The FIRST EVER Starship upper-stage catch
• Ship 42 returning from orbit in good enough condition to be reflown with only minor repairs

For the first time, SpaceX has demonstrated that both stages of Starship can return and be recovered by the launch tower

And Elon confirmed that Ship 42 will likely be preserved for public display because of its historic achievement

“No one has ever taken a stage like that and created a truly reusable upper stage and certainly not brought it back to land propulsively while being caught by giant chopsticks”

Now look at what full and rapid reusability is expected to unlock:

• Up to 100 TIMES lower cost of accessing space
• The potential to deliver MILLIONS OF TONS of payload to orbit annually
• A transportation system where both stages return, refuel, and fly again

That's the scale of what SpaceX is building

Starship has already demonstrated the recovery of both stages. The next step is turning recovery into routine, rapid reuse

And that's what will fundamentally change the economics of spaceflight

Elon Musk reveals how Starlink saved Ukraine from collapse, and sets the record straight on claims he throttled it:

“There is no private individual who has helped Ukraine more than I have. I made sure that Starlink was in Ukraine, prepositioned ahead of the Russian invasion.”

“When Russia invaded, they disabled all communications, all cell towers, all fiber cables, and every satellite communication system. There was one system they could not disable, and that was Starlink.”

“If they had not had Starlink, their entire line would have collapsed because they had no communication system, and Russia would have won. Now, does that sound like a pro-Russian action to you?”

“Even to this present day, Starlink provides the backbone of communications for the Ukrainian military and for Ukraine more broadly. If we were to turn off Starlink, the entire Ukrainian front would collapse immediately.”

“From the beginning, I said that Starlink is a civilian system. It is not meant to be used for offensive drone strikes that kill people. If you want to do that, you need to do Starshield, which is a separate system that is controlled by the US government.”

“In the Starlink system, there is a speed limit. That speed limit is the speed of the fastest road speed limit in Ukraine, which I think is about 80 miles an hour.”

“Do not ask me as a private individual to make kill decisions that sometimes result in the loss of innocent lives, not just soldiers. That is not my position to do. And yet we’ve been pressed relentlessly to do that, which I think is outrageous.”

“Those are the rules that have been in place since the beginning, for years. Now people pressure me to change it, but I’m not changing it.”

"Yeah. So Neuralink, by the way, is obviously, as you mentioned, a private company, much, much smaller. I mean, it's just several hundred people. We now have, I think, over 30 people that have received the Neuralink device. So they have a Neuralink in their head."

Elon Musk reveals what really drives him to make humanity a star-faring civilization: “It’s life insurance, but for everything.”

“If you simply look at the fossil record and look at how many extinction events have happened, which is a lot, then you know that this is simply a matter of time. It’s a when, not an if.”

“We should boldly go like Star Trek, boldly go where no one’s gone before. And perhaps we find some long dead alien civilizations, or perhaps we find actual aliens we could talk to.”

“You know how you can figure out if something’s really cool about the future? Just ask your kid, and they’ll tell you.”

“Life cannot just be about solving one miserable problem after another. There have to be things that excite you and inspire you about the future, that make you happy when you wake up in the morning.”

“You can’t wait to see what happens next. And being a star-faring civilization is one of those things.”

JUST IN: Texas officials have rejected SpaceX's request to advance a property tax break for a proposed $24 billion data center and power plant near Starbase.

Cameron County commissioners voted Tuesday against moving forward with a proposed tax abatement for the project, which would occupy approximately 444 acres near Brownsville, Texas.

According to the company's application, the development would include:

• A $24 billion proposed capital investment.

• A natural gas-fired power plant and advanced computing campus.

• Approximately 500 new jobs.

• An estimated $13.8 billion in taxable property value during its first year.

The vote prevents the requested tax incentive from advancing to a planned public hearing, but does not prohibit SpaceX from proceeding with the development.

The decision comes as SpaceX $SPCX continues expanding its industrial and technology infrastructure around Starbase, its South Texas rocket manufacturing and launch complex.

Elon Musk and Grimes found each other because they both independently made the same obscure joke about an AI thought experiment called Roko's Basilisk. Neither of them knew the other had made it. When they discovered the coincidence, Elon DM'd her. Their first real conversation lasted four hours.

Roko's Basilisk is a philosophical thought experiment about a future AI that punishes anyone who didn't help create it. It's the kind of idea that maybe a few thousand people on Earth find interesting, let alone funny. Elon had tweeted a joke about it. Grimes had made a music video referencing it. Neither one was aware of the other's version.

When someone pointed out the overlap, Elon messaged her. The conversation that followed wasn't flirting. It was two people discovering that their brains worked in the same strange way. AI, simulation theory, the future of consciousness, music as mathematics. Grimes later said she had never met anyone who could follow her thoughts at the speed she was thinking them.

Their first public appearance together was the 2018 Met Gala. They arrived together and the internet lost its mind because nobody could figure out how the richest man in tech and an experimental musician from Montreal ended up in the same universe.

The answer was simpler than anyone expected. They were both the kind of person who makes jokes about obscure AI philosophy at 2am and thinks that's normal. They didn't find each other through fame or fortune. They found each other through a thought experiment that maybe a thousand other people on Earth would have understood.

The rarest kind of connection isn't physical attraction. It's finding someone whose mind works like yours in a world that doesn't understand either of you.

BREAKING: SpaceXSI cuts invoicing time from 24 hours to minutes with Grok Bot.

Five specialized Grok Bots are now handling entire accounting jobs at SpaceXSI, with people stepping in for decisions and approvals:

• Payments: Matches incoming payments to invoices and investigates differences. Work that normally takes an accountant 3–4 hours now takes roughly 30 minutes.

• Customer inquiries: Answers customer billing questions and coordinates requests such as refunds, which still require human approval.

SpaceXSI estimates that handling this workload without Grok Bot would require more than doubling its accounting team. Its accountants can now focus on improving systems and resolving complex issues.

Rocket Lab CEO Peter Beck once said reusable rockets didn't make sense for small rockets like his Electron. He promised he'd eat his hat if he ever changed his mind.

In 2019, with SpaceX already landing rockets, he walked on stage and admitted he was wrong.

Then he explained why he'd doubted it. The rocket comes back at "eight and a half times the speed of sound," through plasma "about half the temperature of the sun," with loads like "three elephants" standing on "a 1.8 mm carbon fibre rocket."

The first two features Matt Palmer walks through in his What's new in Grok Bot 1.0 video this morning, Team Bot improvements and bots that join your meetings, are the same two things I asked for right here on X. On August 30 I wrote that we need to be able to share Grok Bots across teams, and Elon replied "Coming soon." On October 25 I suggested the Grok Bot team let my bot join a Zoom or Teams call with me, or for me, and Elon replied "This might be possible." Meetings started switching on for users less than two weeks later, and now both features lead the 1.0 release.

That says a lot about how responsive this team is. A user describes a need, Elon weighs in himself, and within weeks it is in the product and getting better. Any bot can now become a Team Bot at the flip of a switch, you choose exactly who it is shared with, and a new analytics tab shows the hours it has saved. In a meeting, the bot listens, answers in the chat and picks up spoken instructions, pulling what you need from your connected tools while the meeting is still going. The tempo of Grok Bot's evolution is extraordinary. And these are only two of the many new features in 1.0, so watch Matt's video to see just how fast Grok Bot is improving. I'm grateful to Matt, the team and Elon for listening.

My original asks: https://x.com/TeslaLarry/status/2094146657617072228 and https://x.com/TeslaLarry/status/2114301658259681544

最近硅谷两大佬因为马斯克吵翻了，结果老马亲自下场，一句话把全网看乐了。

先是著名反垄断评论家 Matt 泼冷水：SpaceX 算什么奇迹？马斯克根本不是天才，无非是会找华尔街搞钱，用钞票和工程师硬堆出来的。

这话连平时谁都不服的硅谷传奇程序员 DHH 都看不下去了，直接回怼：太酸了！哪怕你不喜欢马斯克，也得承认他“把吹过的牛变成现实”的能力举世无双。从特斯拉、脑机接口到 SpaceX，世上有一百万个会搞钱的投资人，但只有一个马斯克。

随后马斯克本尊下场，只回了一句灵魂反问：“行，那你给我解释一下蓝色起源、波音和 ULA？”

这一刀，直接捅在了“唯金钱论”的肺管子上。

如果光靠砸钱就能上天，那现在的太空霸主绝不可能是 SpaceX：
1、 比谁更有钱？ 贝索斯的蓝色起源比 SpaceX 早成立两年，背后站着前世界首富，从来不缺钱，结果到现在还在努力追赶。

2、 比谁补贴多？ NASA 当年搞载人航天，同一个任务，给波音砸了 42 亿美元，给 SpaceX 只给了 26 亿。结果 SpaceX 从 2020 年就开始像公交车一样送宇航员上天，波音的飞船却连宇航员都接不回来，最后还得靠 SpaceX 去救场。

3、 比华尔街输血？ SpaceX 起步根本没有华尔街一分钱，全是马斯克卖掉 PayPal 后自己掏的 1 亿美元家底。猎鹰 1 号连炸三次后差点破产，第四次才绝处逢生。

DHH 说得太对了：钱能买来顶级工程师，但买不来“不怕炸火箭”的魄力。

看看星舰第 15 次试飞（Flight 15）就懂了：同一个任务里，助推器在海里丢了，但飞船却从轨道返航、被发射塔的“机械筷子”稳稳夹住。

放在传统航天巨头那里，“丢了助推器”这半句话，就够他们停飞开两年的事故批斗会了；但在 SpaceX，这只是通往成功的又一组实验数据。

@elonmusk 说实话，到底哪个更难造：是一枚能上天的火箭，还是一家“允许工程师靠炸火箭来试错”的公司？

BREAKING: Texas A&M’s $205.5 million semiconductor project will help train America’s next generation of chipmakers for Terafab. 🇺🇸

University leaders say Terafab’s planned chip plant in Grimes County makes A&M’s Semiconductor Institute even more relevant, with Terafab counting on the institute to help attract talent.

• Industry-style facilities: The institute will feature a cleanroom and six laboratories, giving students practical experience with semiconductor technology.

• Construction is progressing: The building is about 20% complete. Substantial completion is expected by the end of 2027, with significant operations planned for mid-2028.

• Infrastructure for long-term growth: Regents just approved $14.2 million for a new well and storage system supporting the RELLIS campus, including the institute.

posts.text:
A lot of people have real trouble thinking about the aggregate behavior of groups. They can only think about individuals.

So they think about Elon Musk as an individual. Maybe they think that he must be retarded, because they need that for emotional reasons. Or maybe they think he is a talented rocket designer.

But even if they realize he understands rockets, they can only think about him as an individual doing tasks. Not about his impact on what the whole company does.

If Elon Musk is just a talented rocket designer, then he can spend all day, every day, improving rocket designs.

But he is just one of 7000 engineers. So even if did a perfect job, he would only improve progress by about .014%

So, when a midwit looks at SpaceX, he sees 7000 engineers, and says to himself "Elon Musk cannot possibly be designing the whole damn rocket himself. These people are giving him too much credit."

This would be absolutely true if Musk were just a some random SpaceX engineer. But he isn't. He's the absolute dictator of the whole damn company.

He decides, with absolute and unquestionable authority, which behaviors are punished and which are rewarded.

Why is this important?

When I worked at Boeing, on various classified projects, I naively came in with the assumption that I was a software engineer, employed to design and build functional software as quickly and cheaply as possible.

Because of this, I focused on functionality and efficiency, for example suggesting changes that would obviate the need for entire projects and software components.

And I very rapidly became persona non grata.

At first, this caused me to adopt an air of aggrieved innocence. I was just trying to do my job well, and I was being punished for it.

Then I gradually came to realize that I hadn't properly understood what my job was, or what the actual mission of Boeing Defense, Space, and Security was.

Boeing DSS was not an aerospace company. Boeing DSS was a fraud company.

Its goal was twofold. First, to maximize transfer of public tax dollars to stockholder pockets. Second, to maintain the appearance of being an aerospace company, to prevent the fraud from being exposed.

Which meant that my real job was twofold. First, to generate billable hours. Second, to look busy.

This is why Space Launch System sucks. Why it is always late when it doesn't fail outright. Why it is at 300% of its target budget. Why it leaves American astronauts stranded and needing a lift from SpaceX.

That's because, for Boeing, building rockets is a side quest. Something they have to do to look busy. Yes, a rocket does occasionally fly, but that's just happening so programs don't get shut down.

For Boeing, coming in early and under budget would actually be failure. The system is functioning exactly as designed.

The cost, not the rocket, is the goal.

Musk and SpaceX don't work like that.

Unlike Boeing executives, Musk is not a useless grifter asshole. He is an entirely different kind of asshole... a rocket obsessed sperg.

So, at SpaceX, engineers do not get rewarded for generating billable hours. They get rewarded for making rockets fly. And for all the subtasks of this, like figuring out how to make rockets lighter, figuring out how to make engines reignite better, figuring out how to make rocket exhaust not destroy launch pads, etc.

And this attracts engineers who care about rockets. You've seen them on broadcasts, crying on open microphones because they dedicated their lives to something and it just flew.

As a rocket engineer, who designs rockets, Musk is probably replaceable. As a rocket company engineer, who designs rocket companies, he is not.

For over 50 years, the US space industry stagnated precisely for the lack of a Musk-like figure, who could not only create an effective aerospace company, but who could thereby demonstrate what an effective aerospace company looks like.

Which makes it much more difficult for fraudsters to get away with fraud.

I'm envious. I wish I could have worked for an aerospace company instead of a fraud company.

But what's more important is that some of us now no longer have to play "who gets the most cheese?".

They get to play "What can we build today?".

posts.name: Elon Musk
posts.text:
What was the significance of this weekend's SpaceX tower catch:

"Catching the second stage is substantially harder than catching the first stage because the Ship returns from orbit while the booster returns from a short suborbital hop. The booster separates minutes after liftoff, performs a brief boostback, and comes back from only a few hundred kilometers away at relatively low speed. Ship must reach orbital velocity, deploy payload, coast for many hours, execute a precise deorbit burn, survive full reentry heating, and only then perform its landing burn. As such, Ship must carry a functional heat shield, fly a long guided atmospheric trajectory from the other side of the planet, and execute a high-energy flip into the “chopsticks” while protecting its heat-shield side. Those combined demands of orbital energy, thermal protection, long-range guidance, and final precision are why a Ship catch is so incredibly difficult. No prior system, including the Space Shuttle, recovered a rocket-style orbital stage in this manner. The catch validates the path to full reusability which is the foundation of Starship’s cost and cadence targets. This is particularly important in driving the economics of orbital data centers." - DB

Morgan Stanley’s Adam Jonas on @SpaceX successfully catching Starship on flight 15:

“In our view, Flight 15 is a historic inflection moment for the company and spaceflight as a whole. SpaceX has recovered three Starship + many hundreds of Falcon 9 boosters in its history, and now others have accomplished the same. However, no entity has ever even attempted to recover a rocket upper stage in history (not counting Space Shuttle) given the intense thermal and mechanical stress of orbital re-entry.

With an upper stage now recovered intact, SpaceX can conduct a deep inspection of Ship 42 and use the findings to improve future vehicles in a way that was never previously possible. We believe it also helps clear the path to ramping full reuse of both booster and ship, the last major technical milestone before weekly or even daily Starship flights become realistic.

With a ship catch, SpaceX has materially de-risked the longer-term TAMs across all 3 of its segments.”

posts.text:
Yes, the green flame is caused by burning copper from depleting fuel in the regenerative cooling circuit and going oxygen-rich (closer to stoichiometric temperature) in the main combustion chamber.

Slight underperformance of engines on this flight is the reason. The booster is meant to land with tiny residuals, so the solution is to improve engine performance and performance consistency (underway with Raptor V3.2), as well as adjust flight software to do MECO1 about one second earlier to ensure enough propellant for boostback and landing (tiny change).

These early ships and boosters are already outdated by improved designs in production or on the test stand, so this booster loss does not change our timeline to reach high volume, fully reusable Starship flights.

BREAKING: SpaceXSI completes MiniHard construction in just ~5 months, with Gun Range targeting a ~4-month build.

According to SemiAnalysis, SpaceXSI is roughly halving construction timelines while most comparable projects face 8–12 month builds.

• MiniHard: Construction finished in approximately 5 months.

• Gun Range: The new site just south of the Tennessee–Mississippi state line is targeting approximately 4 months of construction.

• Colossus 1: Its first retrofit delivered 150 MW of capacity in 122 days.

• Colossus 2: A subsequent retrofit delivered 210 MW in just 91 days.

• Project SPAM: Work started October 5, with the first capacity targeted for December.

• Massive expansion: SemiAnalysis projects the Memphis–Mississippi campus will grow from 0.4 GW of IT capacity in January to 2.4 GW by the end of 2026. That would be a sixfold increase in one year.

• Five major projects: The expansion spans Macrohard, MiniHard, Macroharder, Project SPAM and Gun Range.

• Tesla powering the scale: SemiAnalysis reports 1,377 Tesla Megapacks across Colossus 2, providing nearly 6 GWh of battery storage.

The construction timelines and capacity forecasts are SemiAnalysis estimates, with future milestones still targets.

Elon Musk’s teams are bringing extraordinary speed and scale to the infrastructure powering AI.

posts.name: Elon Musk
posts.text:
SemiAnalysis’s Dylan Patel says Google’s TPUs are just as good as Nvidia’s in his nightly benchmarks, and without Jensen’s wheeling and dealing Google could take a ton of share

“It’s sort of a three-pronged strategy. One is you have to have the technical progress, and that keeps you winning. The second is that you have to have supply chain prowess, and Jensen’s the only executive in the semiconductor industry that is going out there and drinking and meeting and convincing all of these supply chain companies to invest like they’ve never done before, give him the allocations.”

“Now if all of a sudden there’s no Jensen, and Google’s like, actually, double my allocation. The TPU, from our benchmarking, we test TPUs. We run benchmarks on them on open source models every night. They’re just as good as Nvidia. But Google doesn’t have that DNA of wheeling and dealing with the supply chain, wheeling and dealing with customers. Now if that DNA is gone, the thing that is Jensen is gone, does that now mean Google can just take a ton of share? It’s a real big possibility.”

“Same with AMD. Technically, they’re awesome, but they’re just not able to wheel and deal like Jensen is able to. And that’s been a lot of the reason why they’ve been behind. Of course, the software as well. One of Nvidia’s biggest moats being CUDA, and software is being rapidly displaced by the fact that AI models are so good at writing software.”

Dylan Patel says Nvidia’s next CEO has to hold off OpenAI, Broadcom, Google, Anthropic, Meta, Amazon, and AMD chip teams, who are all 'fucking good'

These guys are fucking good. AMD. They’re all really good, and all these startups.”

posts.name: Elon Musk
posts.text:
Zambia has started connecting 751 health facilities across all 10 provinces with Starlink, and the first 90 kits went to Western Province.

There's something poetic about where they started. Every year at the end of the rainy season the upper Zambezi floods the Barotse plain, and for centuries the Lozi king has left his compound at Lealui by royal barge and moved to higher ground at Limulunga. The ceremony is called Kuomboka. In Lozi it means "to get out of water."

Now picture running fiber or building towers across land that turns into a lake for part of every year. A Starlink dish only needs a clear view of the sky, so the water below stops being the problem.

In March 2020, months before Starlink had its first beta users, Elon Musk said it would serve the 3 or 4 percent hardest-to-reach customers, people with no connectivity or really bad connectivity. Six years later, with funding from the Global Fund through Zambia's Ministry of Health, clinics on one of Africa's great floodplains are being brought into the country's electronic health systems from orbit.

posts.name: Elon Musk
posts.text:
Je viens de regarder mon passage dans Quotidien. Évidemment, je suis qualifié d’« influenceur entrepreneur d’extrême droite ».

Déroulons.

Je ne sais pas si vous vous rendez compte à quel point le peuple français vous méprise.

Vous êtes tellement déconnectés du réel que, dans votre petit monde, vous êtes persuadés d’avoir le monopole du bon sens. Alors je vais vous dire ce que vous êtes vraiment. Mais avant, je vais vous dire d’où je parle.

Je suis breton. J’ai grandi dans un système scolaire profondément cassé. La majorité de mes profs étaient de gauche, et la plupart étaient déprimés. Pas méchants. Déprimés. Ils ne transmettaient qu’une chose : la conviction que le monde est injuste, que l’effort ne paie pas, et que demain sera pire qu’hier.

Ce qui m’a sauvé, c’est d’avoir appris seul. J’ai commencé à coder à 12 ans. À 15 ans, j’avais créé un jeu qui me rapportait plus que le salaire de mes profs. Personne ne m’a donné la permission. Personne ne m’a subventionné. J’ai construit, des gens ont joué, j’ai été payé. La leçon d’économie la plus honnête de ma vie.

Ensuite j’ai travaillé dans la tech, j’ai vécu dans la Silicon Valley, j’ai construit pas mal de choses. Et j’ai étudié l’économie par moi-même. Pas pour un diplôme. Pour comprendre comment le monde fonctionne vraiment.

Et surtout, j’ai eu une chance que vous n’aurez jamais. J’ai été connecté, et je le suis encore, aux deux extrémités de la société. D’un côté, les couches les plus modestes, celles que vous prétendez protéger et incarner sans jamais leur parler. De l’autre, les couches les plus hautes : des milliardaires, des bâtisseurs, Elon Musk. Je fais le grand écart tous les jours. Et je peux vous dire une chose : en bas comme en haut, le diagnostic est le même. Vous, vous êtes au milieu, dans le seul étage de l’immeuble qui n’a pas de fenêtre.

Ce que je vais dire maintenant, n’importe quelle personne saine d’esprit qui a un contact avec le réel le comprend.

Yann, tu incarnes un mouvement et des idées qui ne représentent quasiment plus que vous. Ceux qui croient encore Quotidien et ses mensonges répétés en boucle, ce sont deux populations. Les gamins endoctrinés par une école capturée par l’idéologie. Et une partie des Français issus de l’immigration, qu’on manipule en leur répétant que les Français sont racistes. Un récit construit de toutes pièces par cette gauche mortifère, qui a besoin de victimes pour exister et qui les enferme dans ce rôle pour garder leurs voix.

Les idées que vous défendez sont des idées de mort. Elles culpabilisent le travail. Elles humilient ceux qui construisent. Elles transforment chaque citoyen en assisté ou en suspect. Partout où elles ont été appliquées jusqu’au bout, elles ont produit la même chose : la pauvreté, la défiance, l’effondrement. Pas une exception. Pas une.

Je le dis souvent : dans votre camp, il y a les cyniques et les believers. Les cyniques savent que ça ne marche pas, mais ça leur rapporte de l’audience, du pouvoir, des subventions. Les believers, eux, y croient sincèrement.

Yann, je vais te laisser le bénéfice du doute. Je te range dans la case des believers. Alors un conseil : lis Hayek. La Route de la servitude. Ça se lit en un week-end, et ça t’expliquera pourquoi chaque bonne intention que tu défends à l’antenne pave exactement la route que tu prétends combattre.

Tu as sans doute l’impression d’être du bon côté de l’histoire. Ils l’avaient tous. Mais tout ce que tu représentes enverra la France dans le chaos total.

Les gens que tu appelles « extrême droite », ce sont des gens normaux. Des gens qui veulent vivre en sécurité, travailler, être payés dignement pour ce qu’ils font, et élever leur famille dans un pays qu’ils reconnaissent encore. C’est tout. Ce n’est pas une idéologie. C’est le bon sens que vous avez abandonné, puis insulté.

Et je ne sais pas si vous mesurez ce qui est en train de se passer. Les peuples, dans leur intégralité, et avec eux les entrepreneurs, les créateurs de valeur, tous ceux qui font tourner ce pays, commencent à vous détester. Pas à vous critiquer. À vous détester, profondément, viscéralement. Chaque leçon de morale, chaque étiquette, chaque sketch condescendant creuse un peu plus le fossé. Alors un conseil d’ami : calmez-vous. Vraiment.

Je viens d’un milieu très loin des salons feutrés parisiens et des dîners bobos où l’on décide entre soi qui a le droit de parler. Toi, tu vis dans une bulle. Une bulle confortable, chauffée, avec un public qui rit au signal.

Mais le réel ne rit pas au signal.

Plus personne ne vous croit. Et le réel vous jugera. Très sévèrement.

Deep in south Texas, Musk and his team have pulled in some of the most brilliant people on Earth to make space travel as normal and boring as air travel.

The building pictured below is the actual factory where they build Starship, like a car factory for spaceships. You probably wouldn't have guessed it, since it looks like a nice office building. Guten Morgen zusammen,
heute vor elf Jahren, am 13. November 2015, verübten mehrere Attentäter im Namen des Islams, organisierte Anschläge in Paris. Der Horror dauerte über 4 Stunden und forderte 130 Todesopfer sowie knapp 700 Verletzte.

Zuerst sprengte sich gegen 21.17 Uhr ein Selbstmordattentäter in der Nähe des Stadion Stade de France in die Luft und riss dabei einen Menschen mit in den Tod. Der Attentäter wollte eigentlich ins Stadion gelangen. Hier fand gerade ein Freundschaftsspiel zwischen der Deutschen und Französischen Fußballnationalmannschaft vor 80.000 Zuschauern statt. Sein Sprengstoffgürtel wurde jedoch von einem Sicherheitsmann entdeckt, worauf der Attentäter flüchtete. Ein weiterer Sprengstoffattentäter versuchte fast zeitglich ins Stadion zu gelangen, scheiterte ebenfalls und sprengte sich am Toreingang H in die Luft, zum Glück ohne weitere unschuldige Menschen mitzureißen. Beide Attentäter trugen einen gefälschten syrischen Pass mit sich, und beide sollen im Oktober als Flüchtlinge in Griechenland registriert worden sein. Da die Pässe gefälscht waren, ist die Identität der Beiden bis heute nicht bekannt.

Beinah zeitgleich fuhr ein sogenanntes Hit-Team in einem Seat Leon vor eine Bar in einem Pariser Stadtteil. Sie feuerten dort mit Kalaschnikows auf die Gäste, die im Außenbereich saßen. Anschließend schossen sie auf Gäste eines gegenüberliegenden Restaurants. Insgesamt 15 Menschen verloren ihr Leben dort. Nach diesem Anschlag fuhren die Attentäter weiter, erschossen in einem Auto einen Mann und in einem Café, einem Waschsalon und in einem Restaurant noch vier Menschen. Anschließend begaben sich die Attentäter zur Bar "La Belle Équipe". Sie erschossen dort weitere 19 Menschen. 15 Menschen wurden teils schwer verletzt. Ein Selbstmordattentäter sprengte sich in einem Café in die Luft. Die Bombe detonierte unvollständig, weswegen hier keine weiteren Todesopfer zu beklagen waren, 15 Menschen wurden jedoch teils schwer verletzt.

Rund eine halbe Stunde nach dem ersten Attentat am Stadion begann der Horror im Bataclan Theater, wo gerade die US-Band Eagles of Death Metal ein Konzert vor rund 1.500 Zuschauern gab. Zwei Attentäter erschossen zuerst zwei Radfahrer vor dem Theater.
Anschließend drangen sie in das Gebäude ein und schossen mit Kalaschnikows -Gewehren zehn Minuten lang auf die Konzertbesucher. Zusätzlich warfen sie Handgranaten in die Menschenmenge. Einen Angreifer konnten zwei Polizisten töten, mussten sich aber dann wieder zurückziehen und auf Verstärkung warten. Zwei weitere Attentäter nahmen Geiseln und verschanzten sich im Gebäude. Um 0:50 Uhr erfolgte der Zugriff durch die Polizei. Die beiden Attentäter sprengten sich dabei in die Luft. 3 Stunden dauerte das Massaker im Bataclan Theater. 89 Menschen verloren dabei ihr Leben.

Der IS bekannte sich später zu den Anschlägen. Einige der Attentäter kamen als Flüchtlinge getarnt nach Europa. Der mutmaßliche Bombenbauer war zusammen mit zwei weiteren Attentätern kurze Zeit in Ulm. Sie stiegen dort in einem Hotel in der Stadt ab, und wurden dort von einem weiteren Attentäter abgeholt.

Zeugenaussagen von Menschen, die diese Hölle überlebt haben:

„Wir dachten zuerst, es seien Knallkörper. Dann sah es hinten im Saal nach Funken aus. Rasch wurde klar, dass es sich um Mündungsfeuer handelte. Drei Männer mit Gewehren schossen den Zuschauern in den Rücken und stürmten weiter, in die Menge schießend.“

„Das Trio war unvermummt, mit kurzen Bärten. Einer befahl den über tausend Zuschauern, sich auf den Boden zu legen. In akzentfreiem Französisch erklärte er: Ihr habt in Syrien unsere Brüder getötet, jetzt sind wir hier.“

„Sie sagten, wenn ihr euch bewegt, töten wir euch. Sie erschossen die auf dem Boden liegenden Leute trotzdem.“
„Sie töteten, töteten, töteten. Ich war von Toten umgeben. Ich weiß nicht, wie ich überlebt habe.“

„Sie waren schwarz gekleidet. Einer hatte ein sehr jungenhaftes Gesicht, und er ging seelenruhig zur Sache. Er ging sehr methodisch zu Werke, töteten eiskalt einen nach dem anderen.“

„Sein Blut ergoss sich auf mein Bein. Meinen Nachbarn, einen Mann von 50 Jahren, traf ein Schuss direkt ins Gesicht; Stücke seines Hirn fielen auf meine Brille. Ich hörte die Kugeln und versuchte, auf den Boden zu schauen. Da war eine riesige Blutlache.“

„Merkwürdigerweise hört man die Kugeln fast nicht, wenn sie von der Nähe aus abgeschossen werden. Aber ich spürte ihre Hitze an der Wange. Ich war bereit zu sterben. Ich wog damals 122 Kilo, 20 mehr als heute. Wenn einer getroffen wird, dann ja wohl ich.“

„Irgendjemand schaltete das Licht in der Halle an. Keine Ahnung, wer das war. Ich erkannte den Mann, der gerade noch neben mir an der Bar etwas geholt hatte. Er lag am Boden, sein halbes Gesicht war zerstört. Er war tot.“

„Ich lag auf dem Bauch. Meine Freunde waren neben mir. Wir haben langsam und leise geredet. Die Freunde hatten Kinder, ich nicht. Sie hatten mehr Angst als ich. Der rechts sagte: Ich muss meine beiden Kinder wiedersehen.“

„Wenn ein Meteorit irgendwo einschlägt, sind alle sofort tot. Die eigentliche Folter war, dass sie die Leute einzeln erschossen haben. Manche schrien noch Gnade. Schon wurden sie erschossen.“

„Einmal schrie ein Attentäter: Wenn einer nach Hause will, dann jetzt“ Einzelne sind aufgestanden, die wurden gleich erschossen. Auf dem Boden war Blut. Überall waren Tote und Blut.“

„Ich stieg über einen Mann am Boden. Ich nahm seine Hand, doch sie war schlaff und kühl. Ein paar Meter weiter sah ich eine junge Frau, sie war am Rücken getroffen worden. Leute sind auf sie gestiegen. Reflexhaft kauerte ich mich zu ihr, unter uns war eine Pfütze aus Blut.“

„Ich rannte zum großen Boulevard Voltaire, stolperte, verlor meine Brille. Ich drehte mich zurück zu dem Mann, über den ich gestolpert war und wollte mich entschuldigen. Beim Runterbeugen sah ich. Er war tot. Wir sind in ein Wohnhaus geflüchtet und klopften an Türen, aber niemand machte auf. Die Leute hatten Angst.“

„Nach gefühlt einer halben Stunde schrie jemand: Nicht bewegen, sonst schieße ich“

„Dann gab es eine Explosion. Mein linkes Ohr wurde taub davon. Es regnete Blut und menschliche Überreste auf uns.“

„Nach einer Weile kam ein Polizist vom Sondereinsatzkommando zu uns hoch und hielt eine kleine Ansprache, die ich nie vergessen werde. Er sagte: Ich freue mich, Sie alle zu sehen, denn Sie sind Überlebende des Bataclan. Sie sind Helden. Vergessen Sie das nie!“

quote.name: David Sacks

Bombshell story. The spy narrative is collapsing already.

Is there clear & convincing evidence that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy?

- AG says no. (“no conclusions reached”).
- CIA says no. (“not yet convinced”).
- DNI says no (“not entirely accurate and over-torqued”).
- Ranking Democrat on House Intelligence (incoming Chairman) says no. (“today, at least, I don’t know”). This was immediately after he was briefed.

Who argues otherwise? Anonymous officials tell CNN “it strains credulity to believe that she was not acting as an agent of the Chinese government — simply by virtue of the fact that she is a successful Chinese businesswoman working with one of America’s most powerful companies.”

This is their proof after a year of investigating and surveillance? That she was a “successful Chinese businesswoman”?

At this point, the only crime that we know for sure happened is the leaking of the classified memo. Who did that and why?

An investigation should be opened.

In 2014, Elon Musk stood in front of an audience at MIT and told the whole world exactly where AI was going.

Everyone missed it. Because he used one word, and that's the only thing the internet remembered: "demon."

The headlines called him scared of killer robots. Tech blogs called it hyperbole. People moved on.

I went back and watched that moment. It's barely 2 minutes long. You'll never hear the word "AI" the same way again.

Here's what I took away.

1. He called it before almost anyone.

Someone in the audience asks about AI. His face goes serious.

"If I were to guess like what our biggest existential threat is, it's probably that. So we need to be very careful with the artificial intelligence."

This was 2014. No ChatGPT. Most people had never heard the word "chatbot."

2. He asked for rules 12 years ago.

"I'm increasingly inclined to think that there should be some regulatory oversight, maybe at the national and international level, just to make sure that we don't do something very foolish."

National AND international. In 2014.

Governments are still arguing about it today.

3. The demon line wasn't a joke.

"With artificial intelligence we are summoning the demon."

And then the part almost nobody quotes:

"In all those stories where there's the guy with the pentagram and the holy water, it's like, yeah, he's sure he can control the demon. Doesn't work out."

Read that again.

His warning wasn't about the demon. It was about the guy who thinks he can control it.

4. Now here's what got me.

In 2014 he said: summoning the demon.

In 2018 he told Joe Rogan: "Nobody listened."

In 2023 he signed a letter asking AI labs to pause.

In 2026 he told The Economist he can't see any way to stop it anymore. His new philosophy? "Let's enjoy the ride." And: "If you can't beat them, join them."

Today he's building one of the most powerful AIs on Earth.

12 years later, the man who warned us about the guy with the pentagram is holding one.

My takeaway:

He wasn't wrong in 2014. He just realized nobody was going to stop it. So he decided to build it himself.

Whether that's genius or the exact ending of his own story, I honestly don't know.

So now I'm asking you:

Was Musk right in 2014?

Or did he become the guy in his own warning?

Tell me below. I genuinely want to know where people land on this.
